readerTitle: The bonus worked. That was the problem.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (물류 창고, 소프트웨어 고객지원팀) + 실제 기업 (Wells Fargo) + 실제 연구 (Kerr 1975, Gneezy & Rustichini 2000)
insight: 인센티브는 사람들이 일을 '더 하게' 만드는 것이 아니라, 보상받는 부분으로 노력을 '옮기게' 만든다. 그래서 측정하지 않은 부분이 대가를 치른다.
misconception: 보너스가 역효과를 내는 건 직원이 게으르거나 부정직해서다. 문제가 생기면 벌칙 하나를 더하면 된다.

sources.text: Kerr, S. (1975). On the Folly of Rewarding A, While Hoping for B. Academy of Management Journal, 18(4).
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2016). Consent order and press release on Wells Fargo unauthorized accounts.
Gneezy, U. & Rustichini, A. (2000). A Fine Is a Price. Journal of Legal Studies, 29(1).
창고와 고객지원팀 사례 및 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Wells Fargo: CFPB(2016년 9월)는 직원들이 고객 동의 없이 개설했을 수 있는 예금 계좌 약 150만 개, 신용카드 신청 약 56.5만 건을 발표했습니다(합계 약 200만). 카드에는 'about 2 million accounts'로 적었습니다. 이후 조사에서 숫자가 약 350만으로 늘었다는 점도 게시 전 확인하세요. 벌금 액수는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
Gneezy & Rustichini(2000): 이스라엘 하이파의 어린이집 10곳 중 6곳에 지각 벌금 도입, 지각이 늘었고 벌금을 없앤 뒤에도 높은 수준이 유지됨. 카드에는 구체적 배수 없이 서술했습니다. 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
창고 사례 수치(시간당 피킹 25% 증가, 오출고 1%→2%)는 모두 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 2% ÷ 1% = 2배.
Kerr 논문 제목과 게재지(AMJ 1975, 18권 4호)를 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: The bonus worked. That was the problem.
body: A distribution warehouse starts paying pickers a bonus for every order line picked above target. Within a month, picks per hour rise 25%.
Then the returns start arriving. Wrong items, crushed boxes, missing parts. Wrong shipments have doubled, from 1% of orders to 2%. Nobody cheated. Everyone did exactly what they were paid to do.

image.label: Warehouse worker racing past shelves while boxes tumble behind
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 물류 창고 통로에서 작업자가 카트를 빠르게 밀며 달리고, 뒤로 상자 몇 개가 떨어지고 찌그러짐. 머리 위 전광판에 'Picks/hour ▲'. 실제 회사 로고 없음.

cards.title: Picks are up. Errors are up too.
body: You manage the warehouse. The bonus clearly changed behavior, and customers are now complaining about wrong orders.
What do you do next?

options.text: Keep the bonus and add a penalty for each wrong item
options.feedback: It closes one gap fast. But people under pressure find the next gap, like hiding errors or skipping hard-to-reach items.

options.text: Drop the bonus and go back to flat pay
options.feedback: Errors fall, but so does the real speed gain. You learn nothing about what the bonus pushed people to ignore.

options.text: Ask what the bonus made easy to ignore, then reward orders shipped correct and on time
options.feedback: You keep the push for speed but attach it to the outcome you actually want. It takes more work to measure, which is the price.

cards.title: What the bonus counted, and what it didn't.
body: The pickers didn't work harder at everything. They moved effort toward the one thing that paid.

breakdown.label: Hard-to-reach items
breakdown.detail: Slow picks left for the next shift

breakdown.label: Safety steps
breakdown.detail: Time spent on them earned nothing

cards.title: You get what you pay for, not what you meant
body: An incentive **backfires** when it rewards a measure that only partly captures the goal. People shift effort toward the measured part, and the unmeasured part gets worse.
In 1975, management scholar Steven Kerr called this "rewarding A while hoping for B." You hope for accurate, safe, fast shipping. You pay for fast. You get fast.
The narrower the measure and the bigger the reward, the stronger the shift.

image.label: A spotlight on one part of a job, the rest in shadow
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 일을 구성하는 원 다섯 개('Speed', 'Accuracy', 'Safety', 'Care', 'Teamwork') 중 'Speed'에만 스포트라이트와 동전 아이콘. 나머지 원은 그림자 속에서 작아지고 흐려짐.

cards.title: A bank paid for accounts. It got accounts.
body: Wells Fargo set aggressive targets for how many products each customer held, and tied staff pay and job security to them.

In 2016, US regulators found employees had opened about 2 million accounts and credit card applications that customers may not have authorized. The bank fired thousands of staff, but the targets had been set by management.
The lesson isn't only about honesty. A strong reward on a narrow number turned ordinary people toward the number, at the customer's expense.

cards.title: Sometimes the incentive changes what the act means.
body: Economists Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini studied daycare centers in Israel. Some introduced a small fine for parents who picked up children late.
Late pickups went *up*, not down. Parents had felt guilty about being late. The fine turned that guilt into a price, and the price was cheap. When the fine was removed, late pickups stayed high.
So an incentive can backfire two ways: by narrowing effort, or by replacing a sense of duty with a deal.

cards.title: Incentives aren't the enemy.
body: Pay for results works well when the job is simple and the measure covers almost all of it. Piece rates for one well-defined task, with quality checked, can raise output without hidden damage.
Trouble grows when the job has many parts and you pay for one. Before launching a bonus, ask: if someone chased this number and nothing else, what would break?
And plan to revise it. People learn a scheme's gaps faster than you do.

cards.title: Now it's a software support team.
body: You run customer support at a software company. Customers wait too long for answers. You want a monthly bonus for support agents.
Which design is least likely to backfire?

options.text: Bonus for the number of tickets closed
options.feedback: Tickets will close fast, including ones that aren't solved. Users reopen them or give up and churn.

options.text: Bonus for tickets that stay closed for 7 days, plus a monthly review of sample replies
options.feedback: It rewards problems actually solved and keeps human judgment in the loop. It costs time to review, but it's far harder to game.

options.text: Bonus based only on customer satisfaction ratings
options.feedback: Closer to the goal, but agents may avoid hard tickets or ask customers for good scores. One number still invites narrowing.

cards.title: People chase the number. Make sure the number is the goal.
body: An incentive doesn't add effort so much as move it. Whatever you don't measure pays the price.
**Try it today:** pick one target or bonus in your business. Write down what someone could do to hit it while making things worse. Then decide what to add or check.
